Jitters means a feeling of nervousness, anxiety, or unease — the kind you feel right before something important, challenging, or unfamiliar happens.

Think of it as that restless, on-edge feeling in your body and mind when you are about to do something that makes you a little (or a lot) worried. Your stomach might feel tight, your hands might tremble slightly, your heart might beat a little faster. That whole bundle of feelings — that is the jitters.
A Key Thing to Know: It Always Comes With "The"
You almost never say "I have jitters." You say "I have the jitters." The word almost always travels with the word the in front of it. Keep this in mind — it is a fixed habit of the word.
Two Sides of the Same Word

Jitters carries two closely related meanings that often overlap:

1. The emotional/mental side — worry and nervousness about what is coming.

"She had the jitters all morning before her job interview."

This is the most common use. The person feels anxious, unsettled, and cannot fully relax because something stressful or exciting is ahead.

2. The physical side — shaking, trembling, or restlessness in the body.

"Two strong cups of coffee gave him the jitters."

Here, the word describes actual physical shakiness or an unsteady, jittery feeling in the body — often caused by too much caffeine, lack of sleep, stress, or similar things.

In real life, both sides usually happen together: you feel mentally anxious and your body reflects it through shaking or restlessness.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The word slots naturally into a few very common patterns:

"Have the jitters" — to feel nervous

"I always have the jitters before a big presentation."

"Get the jitters" — when the feeling comes over you

"He gets the jitters every time he has to speak in public."

"Give someone the jitters" — when something causes your nervousness

"Loud, sudden noises give her the jitters."
"The thought of flying gives me the jitters."
Common Phrases You Will Hear in Real Life

Because jitters is such a natural, everyday word, people often pair it with the situation causing the nerves:

  • First-day jitters — the nervousness you feel on the first day of a new school, job, or experience.
  • Pre-wedding jitters (or wedding-day jitters) — the anxiety a person feels right before getting married, even when they are happy about it.
  • Pre-game jitters — the nerves an athlete feels before a big match or competition.
  • Stage jitters — the nervousness a performer feels before going on stage (similar to "stage fright").

These phrases are used constantly in everyday English, so recognizing them will help you a lot.
Jitters in News and Financial Language

You will also see jitters used beyond personal feelings. In newspapers and news reports, writers use it to describe collective unease or uncertainty — when a large group of people, investors, or even an entire market feels anxious about something.

"Economic jitters spread across global markets after the unexpected announcement."
"Political uncertainty has caused jitters among investors."

Here, no single person has the jitters — instead, the word describes a widespread mood of worry or instability. This is a slightly more formal, extended use of the word, but the core idea (anxiety, unease) remains exactly the same.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Jitters is an informal, conversational word. It is perfectly fine to use in:

  • Everyday speech
  • Casual writing
  • Journalism and news articles
  • Storytelling and fiction

It would feel out of place in highly formal academic or legal writing, where you would instead use words like anxiety, apprehension, or nervousness. But in most real-world situations, jitters is widely understood and completely natural.
What Makes Jitters Different from Similar Words

• Nervousness is the general feeling. Jitters is a more vivid, physical, and informal way to say the same thing.
  • Anxiety can be long-lasting and deep. Jitters are usually short-term — they come right before an event and tend to go away once it begins.
  • Fear suggests a real danger. Jitters are more about anticipation and uncertainty than actual danger.
  • Butterflies (in your stomach) is a similar informal expression, but it is softer and often used for excitement mixed with nerves. Jitters leans a little more toward pure nervousness or unease.

Jitters are the nervous, uneasy, often slightly shaky feelings you get before something important or stressful — a vivid, informal word that captures both the mental anxiety and the physical restlessness that come with it.
